content: Hammer toe is a deformity that affects the second, third, or fourth toe, causing it to remain permanently bent at the proximal interphalangeal joint, giving it the appearance of a hammer. When the condition involves the distal interphalangeal joint, it is referred to as mallet toe. The underlying mechanism of hammer toe involves an abnormal and permanent bending of the toe at the proximal interphalangeal joint. This occurs due to an imbalance in the muscles, ligaments, or tendons that are responsible for maintaining the toe in a straight position. Several factors increase the risk of developing hammer toe. These include advancing age, being female, having a second toe that is longer than the big toe, and medical conditions such as osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and diabetes. If left untreated, hammer toe can lead to complications. The deformity may become permanent if intervention is not initiated while the toe is still flexible. Additionally, painful corns or calluses may develop as a result of the toes rubbing against the inside of footwear. The condition can arise from various causes that damage the muscles, nerves, or joints of the toe. Common causes include wearing poorly fitting shoes, such as those with excessively high heels or shoes that are too short or narrow. Other contributing factors include osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, stroke, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, and diabetes. Hammer toe typically affects the second, third, or fourth toe. Symptoms include an abnormal bend in the joint of one or more toes, which gives the toe a hammer-like appearance. Movement of the affected toe may be painful or difficult. Additionally, painful calluses or corns may form due to friction between the hammer toe and the inside of the shoe. Treatment for hammer toe can often be managed conservatively. Physical therapy and wearing new shoes with soft, spacious toe boxes are commonly recommended. However, in more severe or long-standing cases, surgical intervention by an orthopedic specialist may be required to correct the deformity. Preventing hammer toe involves choosing appropriate footwear. Shoes should fit properly, have low heels, and provide adequate room for the toes. Avoiding shoes with pointed toes and opting for roomier, adjustable footwear, such as those with laces or straps, can help reduce the risk of developing this condition.
